doc.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024

title: Segregation in the neighborhood and Herbert Delaney
summary: Griffin describes a segregated neighborhood, walking to school with mentor Herbert Delaney, and starting piano with Miss Bessie Marino.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: What was the state of segregation in your neighborhood when you were the age that you’re talking about?

Oh ten or twelve — segregation was very prominent. When I say very prominent, we didn’t see like white people in our neighborhood hardly. None at night. Maybe during the day you might see one or two insurance salesmen or something, but the whole neighborhood was full of black people. And I could go weeks and days without seeing anybody black — I mean white. And, but going to school during the school time we had to pass through a white neighborhood and we never passed through that white

neighborhood solo, alone. Because we would be maybe somebody’d come out and threaten us or run — you know little kids — run at us or something like that. But this guy named Herbert Delaney, he is deceased now, my best friend, my mentor, he was taking piano lessons. He had a piano and his family was — you know he had a mother and a father and his sister went to Alcorn College and everything, but I looked up to him. He was about four years older than me. My stepfather got killed when I was seven years old, and that was the one that told me if I didn’t beat this bully then he was going to beat me and after that I nearly bit the bully’s finger off and he never bothered me again. In fact he acted like he was afraid of me rather than me being afraid of him. He never took any of my marbles, never did anything after I did that. But all that said, around twelve years old I was going to elementary school, I would have to go with Herbert Delaney because he was a bigger guy than me and I looked up to him. And in fact from seven years old through my college and everything he was my mentor. He was my good friend, my mentor, I looked up to him and I took advice from him. He actually, you know, gave me some very precious information about my life and my decisions on life and everything. So, but he had a piano in his house. So the piano lessons started because I had to walk home with Herbert Delaney and he would take his piano lesson, the first lesson he took I think they were 25 cents a lesson or some very — I’d save my money up and I said I’m going to take piano lessons. And then the lady, her name was Miss Bessie Marino, and after a year of taking lessons with her she passed away. She got ill and she died. But I never stopped playing the piano. I was in love with music much earlier than that. In fact you asked me a question about when I really recognized my interest in music. My mother used to sing [sings] Glory hallelujah in a spiritual way. And I would get up in my mother’s lap and tell her to sing Glory and that was my lullaby to go to sleep every night until I did it so long to my mother said, “You’re getting too big for this, you’ve just got to go to sleep.” And I really said, “Mama, sing ‘Glory’ you know, and she would rock in the rocking chair and sing [sings] Glory, glory hallelujah/ Glory, glory hallelujah. And I would go to sleep.
